prompt: You just turned on VoiceOver or NVDA and tabbed to the checkbox from the lesson (a <label> correctly associated via for/id, with aria-hidden="true" applied to it). What did you actually hear announced?

options.text: The checkbox and its label are both announced correctly
Only the checkbox state ('not checked') is announced — no label at all
The label is announced quietly, then the checkbox state
The screen reader skips the control entirely

hints: aria-hidden hides an element and all its descendants from assistive tech — including a label element it's applied to directly.
Programmatic association (for/id) links the label in the DOM, but doesn't make it exempt from aria-hidden.
explanation: aria-hidden="true" on a <label> removes it from the accessibility tree entirely. Even though the label is correctly associated with the input via for/id, a screen reader will only announce the input's role and state ('checkbox, not checked') — the label text is never read, so the user has no way to know what they're checking.

prompt: You just put your mouse aside and tabbed through the lesson's page — a <nav> written after <main> in the HTML, but placed visually above it via flex-direction: column-reverse. Where did your keyboard focus actually go right after the logo?

options.text: Tab order matches the visual order — nav is reached first
Tab order follows the DOM — main is reached before nav, regardless of visual position
The browser automatically reorders tab sequence to match CSS
Focus becomes trapped inside main and never reaches nav

hints: CSS properties like flex-direction change what's rendered where on screen — they don't touch the underlying DOM.
Keyboard tab order is determined by DOM position, not by pixels on the page.
explanation: Tab order always follows DOM order, never visual/rendered order. CSS reordering (flex-direction, absolute positioning, grid order, etc.) can make a page look correct to a sighted mouse user while keyboard users experience a completely different, illogical sequence — main content before navigation, in this case. This is why keyboard testing has to be done by physically tabbing through a page, not just by looking at it.

prompt: What happens to the accessibility tree when aria-hidden="true" is applied directly to a <label> element associated with an input?

options.text: The label and its input become permanently detached; no association survives regardless of for/id or nesting
The label is removed from the accessibility tree entirely — it contributes nothing to the input's accessible name, regardless of for/id association
aria-hidden on a label has no effect because labels are inherently non-decorative
The label remains in the accessibility tree but becomes non-narrated

explanation: Applying aria-hidden="true" to a <label> removes it from the accessibility tree. Even though the for/id association is structurally intact in the DOM, the label contributes no accessible name — a screen reader lands on the input and announces only its role and state (e.g. 'checkbox, not checked'), with no label text at all.

prompt: A web page uses CSS flexbox with 'order: 3' on the first button, 'order: 1' on the second, and 'order: 2' on the third. In what tab order will these buttons receive focus?

options.text: Only the element with 'order: 1' is focusable; others are skipped
First, second, third (DOM source order)
Third, then first, then second (as rendered visually)
Second, then third, then first (CSS visual order)

explanation: Tab order always follows DOM source order unless tabindex is explicitly used to override it. CSS flexbox 'order' affects visual layout but not sequential focus navigation.

prompt: When testing keyboard navigation without a mouse, which behavior confirms correct focus management on a custom dropdown widget?

options.text: Once opened, the dropdown options receive focus only when using Arrow keys; pressing Esc closes the menu and returns focus to the trigger button
Focus moves into the dropdown options on Enter, but pressing Escape does not close it or restore focus
The dropdown options are skipped entirely until Tab is pressed repeatedly many times
Pressing Tab moves focus past the trigger button, and pressing Shift+Tab does not return to it

explanation: Proper keyboard handling requires focus to be programmatically moved *within* the widget using arrow keys while Escape returns control and focus to the trigger element — a testable behavior only by manual keyboard navigation.

prompt: A developer added aria-hidden="true" to the entire <header> section. What effect does this have on screen readers?

options.text: The header's contents are still accessible via landmark navigation (e.g., JAWS + H)
The entire header subtree is excluded from the accessibility tree and not announced
All content in the header becomes narrated with a prefix 'hidden'
Only visible elements inside are hidden; focusable links remain navigable

explanation: aria-hidden="true" on a container removes all descendants from the accessibility tree, regardless of visibility or interactivity. Screen readers will not announce them.

prompt: Which statement about label-input association is *technically* true when testing manually with a screen reader?

options.text: If only the 'for' attribute is present and the 'id' doesn’t match, the input is still labeled by whatever text immediately precedes it visually
A <label> with matching for/id or proper nesting must exist in the accessibility tree to be announced; aria-hidden on it prevents labeling
Screen readers use visual proximity alone to infer labels, so no programmatic association is required
A <label> nested inside the <input>'s parent <div> but not explicitly associated via for/id will still be announced as the input's label

explanation: Labels require either HTML association (for/id or nesting) *and* must remain in the accessibility tree; aria-hidden on a label removes that labeling function.

prompt: A modal dialog's close button receives focus via JavaScript when the dialog opens, and subsequent Tab presses move to interactive elements *inside* the dialog. What must also be true for proper keyboard accessibility?

options.text: Pressing Shift+Tab from the first focusable element should move focus into browser UI or past top of page
Only the close button is focus-trapped; other interactive elements use normal flow
The dialog must trap focus: Tab/Shift+Tab cycle within dialog elements and ignore underlying content until closed
Wrapping only needs to work in the forward Tab direction — it's acceptable for Shift+Tab from the first element to leave the dialog and reach the page behind it

explanation: Focus trapping ensures keyboard users cannot tab to background content while a modal is active, which must be verified by manual keyboard-only navigation testing.

prompt: If an input element has tabindex="0" and a sibling <span> also has tabindex="0", how does focus navigate between them?

options.text: Elements with tabindex="0" are skipped unless explicitly navigated via Tab navigation only once
Focus follows DOM order: whichever appears earlier in the source order gets focus first
Tab order is determined by their visual rendering (e.g., absolute positioning)
Both receive focus simultaneously when clicked, but tab key skips both until next element

explanation: Elements with tabindex="0" are included in sequential focus navigation in DOM order — not visual or rendering order.

prompt: What is the consequence of using aria-hidden on a button that has visible text content?

options.text: The button remains focusable and announced, but only with screen readers that support ARIA
Its parent containers inherit aria-hidden and also become hidden
The button becomes clickable but is not announced to screen reader users
It becomes unfocusable and removed from the tab order entirely

explanation: aria-hidden removes an element from the accessibility tree, so screen readers do not announce it — but the button remains focusable if keyboard-accessible via tabindex or natural placement.

prompt: In a complex page where elements are visually stacked using position: absolute, what determines their tab order?

options.text: The z-index stacking context: lower z-index gets focus first
DOM source order only, regardless of position or visibility settings
The visual layering as seen in browser developer tools (right to left)
Only elements in the topmost z-index layer are focusable; others require mouse click

explanation: Focus order is unaffected by CSS positioning like absolute/flex/grid — it strictly follows DOM source unless tabindex overrides are applied.

prompt: A developer uses aria-label="Close" on a close button, but omits visible text. What is the likely impact for screen reader users?

options.text: aria-label is ignored on buttons; screen readers fall back to inner text or DOM siblings
Visual users see no label, so screen readers should also skip announcing anything
Screen readers will announce 'close, button' only if the button has focusable semantics
The aria-label will be used as the accessible name, but only if the element supports it (e.g., button, link)

explanation: aria-label provides an accessible name if the element supports it (like button), but its absence of visible text may still cause discoverability issues for sighted keyboard users.

prompt: Which test confirms that a carousel's previous/next controls are correctly labeled for screen readers?

options.text: They are skipped during navigation but visible in developer tool inspection
Using screen reader's navigation shortcut (e.g., rotor), the controls appear as 'button' type with descriptive names
Pressing Enter once opens them into a new context before moving again
Pressing Tab reveals them as focusable, and pressing Space triggers movement — but no name is announced

prompt: A checkbox has both a <label> and aria-describedby pointing to additional instructions. How do screen readers typically announce this?

options.text: The full text is concatenated without pause: 'Enable notifications to receive updates about your order'
The screen reader speaks only aria-describedby if present, overriding the label
Label + role + state first, then additional description upon navigation or context change
Only the label text is announced; aria-describedby is ignored unless explicitly navigated

explanation: Screen readers announce the accessible name (label) first, then the description only when explicitly accessed or upon focus entry — not always in a single line.

prompt: If an element's CSS includes pointer-events: none, how does it affect keyboard navigation?

options.text: It remains focusable only if it is a form control like <input> or <button>
It can still receive focus via script or sequential navigation but does not respond to clicks
It becomes non-focusable and is skipped in tab order
The element disappears from the DOM entirely for assistive tech

explanation: pointer-events: none disables mouse interaction but does not affect tab navigation — elements can still be focused via keyboard, requiring programmatic focus handling.

prompt: When an <input> lacks a visible label but has aria-label, what does screen reader testing typically reveal?

options.text: Screen readers announce both inner text and aria-label concatenated
It's not labeled at all unless nested inside <label>
The aria-label serves as the accessible name and is announced on focus or context
The input is announced only with role (e.g., 'edit'), and the aria-label is ignored

explanation: aria-label provides the accessible name even for inputs without visible labels — verified by testing that the label is announced upon focus.

prompt: A page uses JavaScript to dynamically insert a new <button> into the DOM after initial load. When does it become part of the tab order?

When the DOM update completes and it receives standard focusable element attributes (e.g., is not disabled)
Only if explicitly focused via focus() call; otherwise it's hidden from tab order
After a setTimeout of 500ms or longer to ensure accessibility tree sync

explanation: Dynamically inserted elements with native interactivity (e.g., button) become focusable immediately upon insertion — verified by tabbing after DOM mutation.

prompt: A table uses <th> headers but they have aria-hidden="true". What happens when navigating cells with a screen reader?

options.text: Headers are announced after cell data using reverse reference logic
Cells are announced without header context, as if unstructured

The screen reader automatically infers header-cell relationships using DOM position

prompt: Which manual test confirms correct focus order when using CSS to visually reorder elements via 'flex-direction: row-reverse'?

options.text: Tabbing follows DOM order regardless of visual reversing, unless tabindex is overridden
Focus wraps at ends and alternates direction to match visual reversal

Tabbing through items follows visual screen order (right-to-left)

prompt: An <a> element has href="#" and aria-hidden="false". What does that do?

The link becomes focusable only via screen reader virtual cursor, not keyboard Tab
It forces screen readers to announce the link even if it’s empty
It enables assistive tech to navigate only the link, skipping surrounding content

prompt: When testing a progress indicator with role="progressbar", what must be present for accurate screen reader announcement?

aria-label or accessible name via-labelledby, plus aria-valuenow and either aria-valuemax or aria-valuetext
Only aria-valuenow and aria-valuemin are required; aria-valuemax is optional

prompt: Which behavior demonstrates that focus is correctly managed when closing an open modal dialog?

Pressing Esc returns to the triggering button, not the beginning of the document
Focus remains in the modal’s last active element until another tab or click occurs
The entire page receives focus again as a single unit

prompt:
A signup form has two checkboxes, written by two different developers: ```html
``` Only ONE of these two checkboxes will announce a label when a screen reader user tabs to it. Which one is broken, exactly why, and what would VoiceOver or NVDA actually announce landing on it? Then fix the broken markup.
hints: Compare the for attribute on each label against the id on its matching input, character by character — don't assume they match just because they look similar.
Programmatic association via for/id requires an exact string match; even one missing character breaks it completely.
For the broken one, predict exactly what gets announced — compare it to what the lesson's aria-hidden example announced.
explanation: The first checkbox (marketing-opt-in) works fine — for="marketing-opt-in" matches id="marketing-opt-in" exactly. The second is broken: the label says for="sms-opt-in" but the input's id is "sms-optin" (missing the hyphen), so there is no programmatic association at all, despite looking correct at a glance. A screen reader landing on that input announces only "checkbox, not checked" — the exact same silent failure the lesson demonstrated with aria-hidden on a label, just caused by a typo in the id instead. The fix is a one-character change: `<input type="checkbox" id="sms-opt-in">` so the id matches the label's for attribute exactly.

prompt:
Two more checkbox implementations from the same codebase: ```html
``` Which version will screen reader users hear a label for, and which won't? Explain the mechanism for each — don't just say "aria-hidden hides it," explain precisely what happens to the accessibility tree in Version B.
hints: aria-hidden removes the element it's applied to AND every descendant from the accessibility tree — check what's actually a descendant of the aria-hidden element in Version B.
Version A uses a different, also-valid way of associating a label with its input — does the lesson call this technique out by name?
For each version, predict exactly what VoiceOver/NVDA would announce landing on the checkbox.
explanation:
Version A works: wrapping the input inside the <label> element (rather than using for/id) is the third valid association technique the lesson names alongside for/id and aria-labelledby — the label text "I agree to the Terms of Service" is correctly in the accessibility tree and gets announced with the checkbox's role and state.

Version B is broken, and for a subtler reason than the lesson's original example: aria-hidden="true" isn't on the <label> itself here — it's on the <div> that wraps the label. But aria-hidden removes its target AND every descendant from the accessibility tree, and the label is a descendant of that div. So the label is just as invisible to assistive tech as if aria-hidden had been placed directly on it — the checkbox announces only "checkbox, not checked," with zero label, exactly like the lesson's original broken example.

prompt: Two custom checkbox widgets, each pairing a decorative icon with label text: ```html ``` Both widgets use aria-hidden somewhere. One is genuinely accessible; one is broken. Identify which is which, explain precisely what a screen reader announces for each, and state the general rule for when aria-hidden on part of a label is fine versus when it breaks the control entirely.
hints: aria-hidden hides exactly the element it's applied to, plus everything inside it — figure out precisely which element each snippet applies it to.
One developer correctly hid only a decorative icon; the other hid the icon's entire container, including the real label text along with it.
For each widget, ask: after stripping out everything aria-hidden removes, what accessible name is left for the input?
explanation:
Widget 1 is correct. aria-hidden="true" is on the <span> icon only — a legitimate, recommended pattern for suppressing purely decorative content from being announced (without it, a screen reader might read "crescent moon emoji, Enable dark mode, checkbox, not checked" — noisy and confusing). The surrounding label text "Enable dark mode" is not a descendant of the aria-hidden span, so it stays in the accessibility tree, and the label is still properly associated via for/id. VoiceOver announces: "Enable dark mode, checkbox, not checked."

Widget 2 is broken. aria-hidden="true" is on the <label> element itself — the ancestor of both the icon span and the text "Enable compact layout." Because aria-hidden removes its target and every descendant, the entire label subtree — icon and text alike — is pulled from the accessibility tree. The checkbox announces only "checkbox, not checked," with no label at all. The developer likely intended to hide just the icon, like Widget 1, but put aria-hidden on the wrong element.

General rule: aria-hidden on decorative content nested *inside* an accessible label is a good pattern. aria-hidden on the label itself — or on any ancestor that also contains the real accessible text — takes the text down with it and breaks the control.

prompt:
A checkout page uses this HTML and CSS: ```html
``` ```css .button-row { display: flex; flex-direction: row-reverse; /* visually: Continue renders on the left, Back on the right */ } ``` You put your mouse aside and tab through the page. Which button receives focus first — Back or Continue? Is this a bug? If so, fix it, and explain why fixing it with more CSS wouldn't be the right approach.
hints: Tab order is determined by source order in the HTML — never by CSS flex-direction.
Ask: if I only had a keyboard and never looked at the screen, which button would I land on first?
The fix has to happen in the HTML file, not the CSS file — think about why.
explanation:
"Back" receives focus first, because it's written first in the HTML — tab order follows DOM order regardless of flex-direction, exactly as the lesson's nav/main example demonstrated. This is a real bug: a sighted keyboard user sees "Continue" on the left and "Back" on the right (because of row-reverse), so they'd expect Tab to reach Continue first if anything — instead they land on Back first, out of step with the visual order they're looking at. It's invisible to a mouse-only QA pass because the page looks completely correct.

Fix: reorder the actual markup — swap the two <button> elements so <button class="btn-continue"> comes before <button class="btn-back"> in the HTML — so DOM order matches the intended visual/tab order. Patching this further in CSS can never work: flex-direction only ever changes rendering, never the underlying DOM order that Tab actually follows.

prompt:
A footer, with its HTML in this order: ```html
Privacy Terms
Twitter Instagram
``` ```css footer { display: grid; grid-template-areas: "social newsletter legal"; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr; } .social-links { grid-area: social; } .newsletter-signup { grid-area: newsletter; } nav { grid-area: legal; } ``` Visually this shows social links on the left, newsletter form in the middle, legal nav on the right. A teammate says: "It's fine — I put aria-label='Legal' on the nav so screen reader users can jump straight to it with landmark navigation, so tab order doesn't matter here." Is the teammate right? Trace the actual tab order a keyboard user experiences, and explain specifically what the aria-label does and doesn't solve.
hints: Landmark navigation (jumping directly to a labeled region) and sequential Tab navigation are two different ways users move through a page — fixing one doesn't fix the other.
grid-template-areas works exactly like flex-direction and the CSS order property: it changes rendering only, never DOM/tab order.
Trace the actual HTML source order first, ignoring the CSS entirely, to find the real tab sequence.
explanation:
The teammate is only half right. aria-label="Legal" does make the <nav> landmark identifiable and independently reachable for screen reader users who jump directly between landmarks — that part is genuinely useful. But it does nothing for a keyboard-only user tabbing sequentially through the page, and it does nothing to fix the actual tab order.

grid-template-areas, like flex-direction and the CSS order property covered in the lesson, only changes visual placement — DOM/tab order still follows source order in the HTML, which here is: nav (legal links) first, then the newsletter form, then social links. A sighted keyboard user reading left to right expects social → newsletter → legal, but Tab actually delivers legal → newsletter → social — reversed from what they see. The aria-label solves a different problem (targeted landmark jumping) than the one that actually exists (sequential tab order mismatching visual order).

Fix: reorder the markup itself so the DOM sequence is social-links, then newsletter-signup, then nav — matching the visual left-to-right order. The grid-template-areas CSS can stay exactly as-is for layout; it should never be relied on to fix focus order.

prompt:
You're reviewing a pull request that redesigns a pricing table. The diff only touches CSS — it adds `order: -1` to the "Recommended" plan's card so it visually renders first among three pricing cards, without touching the HTML at all. The PR description says: "Moved Recommended plan to the front visually, LGTM to merge."

Write the code review comment you would leave. It must: (1) state precisely what will break for keyboard users and why, (2) say what you'd personally verify by hand before approving — not just what an automated scanner would report, and (3) give the specific fix, including what should change and what should NOT need to change.
hints: Think about what an automated accessibility scanner would and wouldn't catch here — that's exactly why manual testing matters for this class of bug.
CSS order and DOM/tab order are two completely separate systems — changing one never changes the other.
A strong review comment names the specific user-facing symptom (what a keyboard user experiences), not just "this violates a rule."
explanation:
A strong review comment covers:

1. **What breaks**: `order: -1` is a purely visual CSS property — it changes rendering position but never DOM/tab order, which always follows HTML source order. If the Recommended card is still third in the markup, a keyboard user tabbing through the page reaches the other two plans before reaching Recommended, even though it now visually renders first — completely out of sync with what they're looking at. This passes an automated scanner with zero errors, since there's no ARIA or semantic violation here — the only way to catch it is to physically tab through the rendered page (mouse aside) and confirm the sequence you land on matches the sequence you see.

2. **What I'd verify by hand**: I'd tab through the live preview myself and note exactly which card receives focus first, second, third — not trust that `order: -1` did what its name implies for keyboard users.

3. **The fix**: move the Recommended card's markup to be first in the HTML source, matching its new visual position. Once DOM order matches visual order, the `order: -1` can be removed entirely — don't stack another CSS property on top to patch a problem that only exists because the source order itself is wrong.

hints: Trace both directions separately — Tab forward from the last element, and Shift+Tab backward from the first element — don't assume the code handles them symmetrically.
Look at exactly what the keydown handler checks: does it ever read e.shiftKey anywhere?
A real trap has to intercept the boundary case in both directions, not just one.
Split the lifecycle into two separate moments and check each independently: what happens the instant the modal opens, and what happens the instant it closes.
Is anything in openModal() actually moving focus into the dialog, or does it just make the dialog visible?
document.body isn't focusable by default — think about what calling focus() on it actually accomplishes.
Don't just re-check the Tab-wrap logic — it's already correct here. Look at every interactive-looking element and ask: can I actually reach it and activate it using only a keyboard?
The 'focusable' NodeList only queries for 'button' elements — check whether every clickable-looking element in the markup is actually a <button>.
Check every place closeModal() is wired up — is there a keydown listener for Escape anywhere, or only onclick attributes?
explanation:
Two real problems remain, even though the trap logic and focus restoration are both solid:

1. **The close "×" is unreachable by keyboard.** It's a `<div class="close-x" onclick="closeModal()">`, not a <button> or <a href>. Divs aren't natively focusable or keyboard-operable — no default tabindex, no keydown-triggered click. Worse, `focusable` is built with `querySelectorAll('#delete-modal button')`, which only matches real <button> elements — the close div isn't in that NodeList at all, so it's silently excluded from the tab cycle entirely. A mouse user sees and can click the × fine; a keyboard user can never reach it and has no way to know it exists, because Tab just cycles between Delete and Cancel.

2. **There's no Escape key handling anywhere.** closeModal() is only ever wired to onclick attributes. A correctly-implemented dialog should close on Escape and return focus to the trigger — here, Escape does nothing at all, even though clicking Cancel and the trap wrapping both work.

Fix priority: the unreachable close button first — it's a complete "this functionality doesn't exist for keyboard users" gap (either give the div `tabindex="0"` plus a keydown handler, or, better, make it a real <button> and include it in the `focusable` NodeList so the trap wraps around it too). Escape-to-close is the close second priority — genuinely expected behavior that's simply missing, but Cancel and Delete remain independently reachable via Tab, so it's a smaller gap than a control that's completely unreachable.

prompt: A Havenmark product page has a "Free shipping over €50" banner rendered in a slightly lighter shade of the brand's already-light grey — you measure it at 2.8:1 contrast against its background, well under the 4.5:1 minimum. A teammate argues it's just an inconvenience because "you can still read it if you look closely." What's the strongest reason this is a barrier, not an inconvenience?

options.text: The task-completion test applies here — a defined class of users (low vision, situational glare, older users) cannot reliably read it at all, which is a different outcome than everyone reading it with slightly more effort
Any WCAG failure is automatically a barrier by definition, regardless of what it actually prevents anyone from doing
It's a barrier because the teammate's opinion that it's minor doesn't count as expert judgment
It's only a barrier if a real user files a complaint about it

hints: The test isn't whether the text is readable in principle — it's whether it's reliably readable for a defined population versus another.
"Looking closely" is doing a lot of work in the teammate's argument — ask who that costs more, and by how much.
explanation:
Correct answer: the task-completion test is what makes this a barrier — a defined class of users (low vision, older users, anyone viewing the page in bright light) can't reliably complete the task (read the shipping threshold) at all, while a full-vision user in good lighting reads it without noticing anything wrong. That asymmetry is the barrier, not the raw fact of a failed contrast ratio.

Why the distractors attract: "any WCAG failure is automatically a barrier" sounds like a safe, rule-following answer, but it skips the actual reasoning the lesson teaches — citing a criterion is necessary but the barrier test is about who gets blocked, not just which rule number applies. "It's a barrier because the teammate is wrong" replaces a testable claim with an appeal to authority, which is exactly the kind of finding that collapses under scrutiny in a client review. "Only a barrier if someone complains" inverts the whole point of auditing — the job exists specifically to find barriers before a user has to discover and report them.

prompt: Havenmark's checkout has a "Complete your order in 09:58" countdown timer with no way to pause, extend, or disable it. Which category of access need does this finding primarily protect, and which WCAG success criterion governs it?

options.text: Vision — SC 1.4.3 Contrast Minimum
Cognitive, chronic-pain/fatigue, and motor access needs together — SC 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable
Vestibular — SC 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions
Hearing — SC 1.2.2 Captions (Prerecorded)

hints: Ask who specifically runs out of time on a form that a fast, unaided user finishes in under two minutes.
This finding isn't about how the timer looks or sounds — it's about what it does over a duration.
explanation:
Correct answer: a rigid time limit disproportionately burdens several overlapping access needs at once — someone whose cognitive processing means re-reading a field takes longer, someone whose chronic pain or fatigue means they need to pause mid-task, and someone whose motor condition means typing takes longer or requires more corrections. SC 2.2.1 (Timing Adjustable, Level A) is the criterion that governs exactly this: time limits must be adjustable, extendable, or removable, unless the timing is essential (which a shopping cart hold is not).

Why the distractors attract: contrast (1.4.3) is a real WCAG criterion but it's about visual perceivability of text against background, not duration — it's the wrong axis entirely, chosen because it's the most familiar SC number from earlier lessons. Animation from interactions (2.3.3) is genuinely relevant to vestibular access needs discussed in the same lesson, which is exactly why it's tempting here — but a static countdown number with no motion or parallax doesn't trigger it; the harm here is duration, not movement. Captions (1.2.2) is a real criterion for an entirely different modality (audio/video) that has no connection to a checkout timer at all — included as the option a learner who hasn't done the reading might grab at random.

prompt: Havenmark's axe-core CI run reports zero critical issues on a page where the size-picker is six unstyled <div> elements with click handlers, completely unreachable by keyboard. What's the most accurate way to describe what the scan result actually tells you?

options.text: The scan is broken and needs to be replaced with a better tool
The page has no accessibility problems the scan is capable of detecting — which is a narrower claim than "the page is accessible"
The page is fully accessible, since a zero-error scan is the industry-standard bar for conformance
The scan result is meaningless and shouldn't be trusted for anything

hints: The scan is answering a real, narrower question — figure out exactly what that question is before deciding whether the result is wrong.
"Zero errors reported" and "zero errors exist" are two different claims — only one of them the scan can actually support.
explanation:
Correct answer: a scanner reports on the roughly one-third of WCAG success criteria it can verify by parsing markup — syntactic and structural checks. "Zero critical issues" accurately describes the result of that narrower check; it does not and cannot mean "this page works for everyone," because keyboard operability of a custom widget requires simulating an interaction sequence over time, which is outside what a static-DOM scan does.

Why the distractors attract: "the scan is broken" blames the tool for a limitation that's structural to every automated scanner, not a defect in this one — axe-core is doing exactly what it's built to do, correctly. "Zero errors is the industry-standard bar for conformance" is the exact misunderstanding that let this bug ship — it treats a triage tool's clean result as equivalent to a conformance claim, which is precisely the gap this lesson exists to close. "The scan result is meaningless" overcorrects in the other direction — the scan genuinely did catch a real category of issues (the syntactic third), and dismissing it entirely would mean re-checking things it already verified reliably.

prompt: Which pair of findings correctly illustrates the difference between a barrier and an inconvenience?

options.text: Barrier: a submit button at 2.9:1 contrast that fails SC 1.4.3, blocking low-vision users from locating it. Inconvenience: the same button's corner radius doesn't match the design system's other buttons
Barrier: a page loads 200ms slower than average. Inconvenience: a form field has no visible label at all
Barrier: the auditor personally dislikes the site's color scheme. Inconvenience: a modal traps keyboard focus incorrectly
Barrier: an image has verbose alt text. Inconvenience: an image has no alt text at all

explanation: The correct pairing puts a measurable, task-blocking failure (contrast under the WCAG minimum, preventing a defined group from locating a control) against a genuinely cosmetic mismatch (corner radius) that doesn't block anyone. The other three options invert the categories — pairing a real defect (missing label, focus trap failure, missing alt text) with the "inconvenience" side, or putting personal taste and minor performance variance on the "barrier" side where they don't belong.

prompt: Under the social model of disability, where does an accessibility defect "live"?

options.text: In the user's body or condition, which the design should accommodate as a special case
In the mismatch between the design and the range of bodies and minds using it — the environment is what disables
Nowhere specific — disability is purely a medical diagnosis unrelated to design
In whichever party is easiest to ask to change, regardless of who actually built the barrier

explanation: The social model locates disability in the mismatch between a design built for an assumed "typical" user and the actual range of users encountering it — the barrier is in the environment, not a deficit in the person. The medical-model option is the contrasting frame the lesson explicitly warns against, tempting because it's the more common default framing in casual conversation. "Purely a diagnosis" ignores both models entirely. "Whichever party is easiest to ask" sounds pragmatic but has nothing to do with either model — it describes expediency, not where a defect actually originates.

prompt: A defect ticket reads: "Deaf users can't use the video since it has no captions." Rewritten in social-model language, which version is most accurate and most likely to get scheduled?

options.text: "Video has no captions (fails WCAG 1.2.2, Level A) — unusable for deaf and hard-of-hearing users, and for anyone in a sound-off environment; add synchronized captions"
"Some users have reported difficulty with this video and would like captions added if convenient"
"Deaf users are unable to access video content and should use an alternative format instead"
"Video accessibility could be improved for a small number of affected users"

explanation: The correct rewrite cites the failing criterion, names the mechanism (no captions), states the full population affected including a situational group (sound-off environments), and gives a concrete fix — the shape the lesson defines as a defect report rather than an accommodation request. The other three options all soften the finding into optional, minor, or user-relocated language: "if convenient" and "could be improved" downgrade a Level A conformance failure to a suggestion, and "should use an alternative format" puts the burden of working around the bug back on the excluded user instead of on the design.

prompt: A tap target on a mobile checkout page measures 22×22 CSS pixels. WCAG 2.2's SC 2.5.8 (Target Size Minimum, Level AA) sets a floor of 24×24 CSS pixels. What's the correct classification of this finding?

options.text: A barrier — it falls under a specific, named success criterion with a measurable numeric threshold the target fails
An inconvenience, since 22px is very close to 24px and the difference is imperceptible to most users
Not a valid finding, because target size is a mobile-design best practice rather than a WCAG requirement
A barrier only if a specific tester with a motor condition happens to miss the target during testing

explanation: It's a barrier because it fails a specific, numeric Level AA success criterion — no additional evidence is required beyond the measurement itself to file it. "Close enough" treats a hard numeric threshold as a matter of degree, when the criterion doesn't have a sliding scale — 22px fails exactly as 10px would, just by less. "Not a valid finding" is simply incorrect: SC 2.5.8 was added specifically because target size had been treated as design opinion rather than a testable requirement, and this criterion exists to end that ambiguity. Requiring a tester to visibly miss it during a session confuses evidence-gathering with the underlying rule — the criterion doesn't require a failed attempt to be filed, though a failed attempt is strong supporting evidence when you have it.

prompt: Which of the following is a genuinely situational (not permanent or chronic) access need an audit should still account for?

options.text: A user viewing a phone screen in direct outdoor sunlight, unable to make out low-contrast text they could read fine indoors
A user with a permanent visual impairment using a screen reader every day
A user with chronic fatigue who needs to pause mid-task on most days
A user with a lifelong tremor affecting fine motor control

explanation: Outdoor glare is the textbook situational case — a temporary environmental condition that produces the same functional barrier (can't read low-contrast text) as a permanent low-vision condition, without being permanent or chronic itself. The other three options are real, important access needs the lesson also covers, but they're permanent or chronic conditions, not situational ones — they're included as plausible-sounding wrong answers because all four genuinely belong in an audit's scope, just not under the specific label "situational" this question asks about.

prompt: A product page uses dense phrases like "Expedited Tier 2 Fulfillment" with no plain-language explanation. Which WCAG success criterion category and access need does this primarily map to?

options.text: SC 3.1.5 Reading Level — cognitive access need
SC 1.4.3 Contrast Minimum — vision access need
SC 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable — chronic-pain/fatigue access need
SC 2.5.8 Target Size Minimum — motor access need

explanation: Dense, jargon-heavy copy with no plain-language alternative is a reading-level and comprehension issue — SC 3.1.5, a cognitive-access finding. The contrast option is tempting only because it's the most-repeated SC number across this module's earlier examples, but contrast is about visual perceivability of rendered text, not about the complexity of the words themselves. Timing and target-size are both real criteria covered in this module, included here because their numbers are fresh from other lessons — but neither has any connection to unexplained jargon.

prompt: An auditor with chronic fatigue tests a five-step checkout form that can't be saved partway through — closing the tab mid-form loses all entered data. There's no single WCAG success criterion titled "fatigue." What's the correct conclusion?

options.text: This isn't a valid accessibility finding, since no WCAG criterion is specifically about fatigue
It's still a real, filable finding — it maps to error-tolerance and timing-adjacent criteria (like SC 3.3.4) even without a criterion named after the condition itself
It's a valid finding only if the auditor can prove a majority of users share this need
It should be filed as a general usability suggestion rather than an accessibility defect, since no SC number applies cleanly

explanation: Chronic-pain and fatigue findings often don't map to one cleanly-named SC the way contrast or alt text do — but that doesn't make them invalid; they map to related criteria (error prevention/recovery, timing) and to the general WCAG principle of operability for users who can't sustain continuous interaction. "Not a valid finding" and "file as general usability" both make the mistake of treating "no single matching SC title" as "not an accessibility issue," which would erase an entire category of real, lived-experience findings this module exists to teach you not to erase. "Only valid if a majority share the need" reintroduces the population-size argument the lesson explicitly rejects — SC-based findings don't require majority-affected status to be legitimate.

prompt: A parallax-scrolling homepage section triggers real dizziness and nausea in some users during testing. Which access-need category does this primarily belong to, and what's the practical mechanism a site can implement to address it?

options.text: Vestibular access need; honoring the prefers-reduced-motion media query so users who've set that system preference don't get the motion
Cognitive access need; simplifying the page's reading level
Motor access need; enlarging the tap targets in that section
Hearing access need; adding captions to the section

explanation: Motion-triggered dizziness and nausea are the defining symptom of a vestibular access need, and prefers-reduced-motion is the concrete, implementable mechanism (an operating-system-level user preference a site can detect and honor via CSS/JS) — not a vague "be more careful with animation" gesture. The other three options each name a real access-need category and a real mitigation from elsewhere in this module, but none of them addresses motion sensitivity specifically — they're included because a learner skimming for keywords like "access need" and "mechanism" could match the pattern without matching the actual symptom described.

prompt: A product manager says: "Our voice-control users are such a tiny fraction of traffic, let's deprioritize the aria-label mismatch bug." What's the most accurate accessibility-QA response?

options.text: Traffic share doesn't determine whether SC 2.5.3 (Label in Name) is a conformance requirement — and voice-control use spans permanent motor conditions, temporary injury, and situational hands-busy use, which is broader than the PM's traffic estimate likely captures
Agree to deprioritize it, since traffic data is the most objective way to rank accessibility bugs
Escalate by threatening legal action rather than explaining the finding
Concede the point but ask for a UX-polish ticket instead of an accessibility fix

explanation: The strongest response does two things: names that conformance requirements aren't scaled by traffic share (a Level A/AA criterion doesn't become optional at low usage numbers), and broadens the PM's likely undercount of who uses voice control — permanent motor conditions, a temporary wrist injury, or someone holding a baby with hands-busy for a session are all real voice-control use cases, exactly as this lesson's situational-needs section describes. Agreeing based on traffic data concedes a frame the lesson explicitly rejects. Threatening legal action skips past the actual technical conversation and burns the relationship without making the case. Converting it to a UX-polish ticket, like the medical-model example earlier in this module, downgrades a defect into a preference.

prompt: Which of the following is an automated scanner reliably able to detect on its own?

options.text: An element with no alt attribute present at all
Whether an image's alt text accurately describes what's in the image
Whether a custom-built dropdown widget responds correctly to arrow-key navigation
Whether a modal dialog's focus trap wraps correctly in both the Tab and Shift+Tab directions

explanation: A missing alt attribute is a pure structural check — the attribute either exists or it doesn't, which a scanner determines by parsing the DOM with no need to understand meaning. The other three all require judgment or simulated interaction over time: evaluating whether text accurately describes an image needs image and language understanding no rule-based scanner has; verifying arrow-key behavior on a custom widget requires actually sending keystrokes and checking behavior; verifying a focus trap in both directions requires the same kind of interaction simulation the earlier modal lesson covered by hand.

prompt: A team wants to replace all manual accessibility testing with a nightly automated scan, citing the scan's zero-error result as proof the site is fully conformant. What's the strongest argument against this plan?

options.text: Automated scanners verify roughly a third of WCAG success criteria by structural pattern-matching; the rest — keyboard operability, label quality, focus behavior, timing, motion — require a human operating real assistive technology
Automated scans are unreliable and frequently produce false positives, so their results can't be trusted at all
Manual testing should replace automated scanning entirely, since automation adds no value to an audit
The scan should run more frequently — hourly instead of nightly — to catch the gap

explanation: The strongest argument states the actual structural limit — roughly one-third coverage, and specifically what kind of issue falls outside that coverage — rather than a vague objection. "Scans produce false positives so can't be trusted" mischaracterizes the actual problem, which is coverage, not accuracy, and would wrongly suggest fixing the scanner's precision would solve this. "Manual testing should replace automation entirely" overcorrects — the lesson explicitly says running scanners in CI is good practice for the third of issues they do catch well. Running the same scan more frequently doesn't expand what it's capable of detecting — frequency and coverage are unrelated variables.

prompt: In a well-sequenced audit workflow, what is the correct purpose of running an automated scan first?

options.text: To triage the high-volume, structurally-detectable issues quickly, so manual keyboard and screen-reader passes aren't repeatedly interrupted by things a machine already caught
To produce the final conformance verdict, since a passing scan is the end goal of an audit
To replace the need for testers with lived experience, since the scan covers the same ground more consistently
To generate a list of findings to hand directly to the client with no further review

explanation: The scan's correct role is triage — clearing the syntactic, high-volume issues out of the way first so the more expensive manual passes can focus on what only a human can find. Treating it as the final verdict, a replacement for lived-experience testers, or a client-ready deliverable all mistake the scan's narrow, real value (roughly a third of the picture, fast and consistent) for the whole audit — exactly the mistake Havenmark's dev team made with their CI scan in this lesson's hook.

prompt: A heading structure on a page is technically valid — no skipped levels, correct nesting — but doesn't represent the actual content hierarchy a sighted reader would perceive from the page's visual structure. Why does this evade an automated scan?

options.text: Valid nesting and semantic accuracy are two different checks; a scanner verifies the first (a syntactic rule) but has no way to judge whether headings represent meaning correctly (a comprehension task)
Scanners don't check heading structure at all, valid or otherwise
This can only be found by a screen reader, never by a scanner or a sighted manual reviewer
Heading structure isn't covered by any WCAG success criterion, so there's nothing for a scanner to check

explanation: Scanners do check heading nesting validity — that part is real and useful — but "correctly nested" and "correctly represents the content" are separate questions, and only the first is structurally checkable by a rule. "Scanners don't check headings at all" is factually wrong — most scanners do check nesting. "Only a screen reader can find this" overstates the case — a sighted manual reviewer comparing the heading outline against the visible content structure can catch this too, without needing a screen reader specifically. Heading structure absolutely is covered by WCAG (SC 1.3.1, 2.4.6), so "nothing to check" misstates the standard.

prompt:
You're auditing Havenmark's size-guide page and find two things worth noting:

1. The page's "Fit tips" section is written in a friendly, casual tone some readers might call informal.
2. The same section's expandable "How to measure" accordion has a chevron icon that rotates on open/close, implemented purely with a CSS `:hover` and `:focus-within` state on a wrapping `<label>` — there is no `<button>`, no `aria-expanded`, and no way to trigger it from a screen reader's virtual cursor or from Tab-only navigation without a mouse hovering.

Write up both findings as they should actually be classified — barrier or inconvenience — and for the one that's a barrier, write it in social-model language with a cited WCAG success criterion, the way this lesson's Draft B example does it.
hints: Apply the task-completion test to each: does either one block or meaningfully burden a defined class of users relative to everyone else?
CSS-only interaction states like :hover and :focus-within often silently exclude touch and keyboard-only users — trace exactly who can and can't trigger this accordion.
For the barrier, follow the lesson's Draft B structure: name the failing criterion, the mechanism, the full population affected, and a fix.
explanation:
Finding 1 (informal tone) is an inconvenience, not a barrier — tone is a stylistic preference, and no defined class of users is blocked from reading or understanding friendly, casual copy relative to anyone else. It might be worth a content-style note, but it isn't an accessibility defect.

Finding 2 (the CSS-only accordion) is a genuine barrier. Written in social-model language with a cited criterion: "The 'How to measure' accordion is triggered only by :hover and :focus-within on a wrapping <label>, with no <button> element, no keyboard activation path, and no aria-expanded state — fails WCAG 4.1.2 (Name, Role, Value) and functionally fails 2.1.1 (Keyboard, Level A). Unusable for keyboard-only users, screen reader users navigating by virtual cursor (who can focus into the label but have no way to 'activate' a hover-only trigger), and touch-only mobile users, since touch doesn't produce a persistent :hover state either. Fix: rebuild as a real <button> with aria-expanded reflecting open/close state, controlling a linked content region via aria-controls." Note that this framing correctly identifies the affected population as broader than one group — it costs keyboard users, screen reader users, and touch users independently, for the same underlying implementation choice.

prompt: A Havenmark engineer, after reading your ticket about the discount badge's low contrast, replies: "I get that it's a WCAG failure, but practically speaking, almost nobody is actually blind — is this really worth a sprint slot over the three feature bugs also in the queue?" Using the medical vs. social model distinction and the task-completion test from this lesson, write the response you'd actually give in that thread. It should correct the specific misconception in the engineer's framing, not just restate that WCAG compliance is required.
hints: The engineer's objection assumes the affected population is 'blind users' specifically — check whether that's actually who a 3.2:1 contrast failure affects.
Avoid just citing the rule again — the engineer already knows it's a WCAG failure and doesn't find that persuasive on its own.
Name the actual population, using the social-model framing, the way the lesson's Draft B example does.
explanation: A strong response corrects the underlying misconception rather than just repeating the rule: the badge's 3.2:1 contrast failure has almost nothing to do with blindness specifically — a blind user relying on a screen reader doesn't perceive contrast at all, because they're not reading the badge visually in the first place. The population actually blocked by this bug is low-vision users, older users (contrast sensitivity declines with age for most people, independent of any diagnosed condition), anyone with a scratched or glare-affected screen, and anyone viewing the page in bright light — a considerably larger and more varied group than "almost nobody" suggests, and one that includes a meaningful share of Havenmark's actual customers on any given day, not a rare edge case. This reframes the engineer's mental model from medical (a specific, rare diagnosis) to social (an environmental mismatch that a much broader range of everyday viewing conditions triggers) without needing to re-argue that WCAG compliance matters — it corrects who's actually affected, which is the part the engineer got wrong.

prompt: Design the manual testing pass you'd personally run on Havenmark's checkout flow to cover access needs beyond vision alone — motor, cognitive, vestibular, and chronic-pain/fatigue. For each of the four categories, name one concrete thing you'd check on this specific flow (not a generic checklist item) and the WCAG success criterion or mechanism it maps to. You don't need a screen reader for this pass — say so explicitly, and explain why not.
hints: Ground each check in something Havenmark's checkout actually has — the countdown timer, the carousel, the quantity stepper, the multi-step form — not a generic textbook example.
For each category, ask: what would make this specific task cost more, or fail outright, for someone in that category?
State explicitly which of the four checks require a screen reader and which don't — most of them don't.
explanation:
A strong answer names four concrete, flow-specific checks, roughly like: **Motor** — measure the quantity stepper's tap targets against the 24×24px SC 2.5.8 minimum, and try completing checkout one-handed with a trackpad only, no keyboard shortcuts. **Cognitive** — time how long the shipping-address step actually takes on a high-effort day versus reading it fresh, and check whether the form preserves entered data if a field validation error interrupts the flow (SC 3.3.4 territory) rather than clearing progress. **Vestibular** — check whether the "customers also viewed" carousel's motion responds to the `prefers-reduced-motion` system setting, and whether it can be paused manually regardless (SC 2.2.2). **Chronic-pain/fatigue** — check whether the session timeout gives a warning before it fires and an easy way to extend it (SC 2.2.1), and whether the flow can be abandoned and resumed later without losing entered data.

None of these four require a screen reader — that's the point worth stating explicitly: this lesson's whole argument is that the vision-and-screen-reader case is one category among several, and a tester can run a complete, high-value pass on motor, cognitive, vestibular, and chronic-pain/fatigue access needs using nothing but a keyboard, a stopwatch, a trackpad, and their own body's response to the flow.

prompt: You log a finding: "Tested the checkout timer on a day with heavy brain fog — a form that should take under two minutes took me 14, including two full re-reads of the shipping section. Recommend removing the fixed timeout or replacing it with a warn-and-extend pattern." A reviewer asks you to "depersonalize" the finding by removing the first-person testing note before it goes in the client report, arguing it's "not professional" to include. How do you respond, and what — if anything — do you actually change in the write-up?
hints: Separate two different questions: is first-person testimony valid evidence, and does the client-facing report need the same wording as your internal testing notes?
Consider what's lost if the concrete 90-seconds-to-14-minutes data point is removed entirely versus just reworded.
This track's whole premise is that lived-experience testing is the differentiator — think about what conceding "not professional" would actually concede.
explanation:
A strong response separates two things the reviewer has bundled together: whether first-person lived-experience testimony is valid evidence (yes, unambiguously — it's some of the strongest evidence available, precisely because it's a reproducible measurement of a real cognitive-load state rather than a guess about what "a cognitive user" might experience), and whether the client-facing report needs the exact same phrasing as internal testing notes (a fair, separate question worth actually agreeing on).

What should not change: the concrete data point — a 90-second task taking 14 minutes under a specific, real, reproducible condition — because that specificity is what makes the finding falsifiable and credible, rather than a vague claim that "some users might need more time." Removing it to sound more "professional" would strip out the strongest evidence in the ticket and replace it with something weaker.

What could reasonably change: the framing, if needed, from strictly personal ("I took 14 minutes") to testing-methodology language ("testing under simulated high-cognitive-load conditions showed task time increase from ~90 seconds to 14 minutes") — while keeping every bit of the concrete measurement. The response to the reviewer should make clear that "professional" and "first-person" aren't in tension: this track's entire premise is that testers bringing their own access needs to the work produce findings a purely simulated or purely able-bodied review can't, and treating that as something to hide rather than a credential undermines the report's actual authority.

prompt: Havenmark's engineering lead proposes a compromise: "What if we just add more axe-core rules to catch the stuff you keep finding manually — the keyboard trap issue, the useless alt text?" For each of those two specific bugs, explain whether a more thorough automated rule set could actually catch it, and why or why not. Be precise about the mechanism, not just "scanners can't do that."
hints: For each bug, ask what information the scanner would need to detect it, and whether that information is derivable by parsing a single static DOM snapshot.
One of the two might be partially closeable with a smarter rule; the other has a harder ceiling. Figure out which is which and why.
Think about what 'useless' alt text actually requires understanding, versus what 'keyboard trap' requires simulating.
explanation:
The two bugs have different ceilings, and a precise answer should distinguish them rather than lump them together.

**Useless alt text** (e.g. `alt="image_047.jpg"`) has a genuinely hard ceiling for rule-based detection: telling good alt text from bad requires understanding what's in the image and whether the text describes it — a task that needs image understanding and language comprehension, not DOM parsing. A rule can flag suspicious patterns (alt text that looks like a filename, alt text under three characters, alt text identical to the image's src attribute) as heuristics, and that's worth doing — but it will always have false negatives (bad-but-not-filename-shaped alt text passes) and occasional false positives. It moves the needle, it doesn't close the gap.

**Keyboard trap / focus escaping a modal** has a different, more tractable ceiling: this could, in principle, be caught by a more sophisticated tool that actually simulates keypresses — some modern tools do attempt exactly this (automated interaction-simulation testing, as opposed to static DOM analysis). But it requires a fundamentally different kind of tool than a markup-parsing scanner: one that opens the modal, dispatches Tab and Shift+Tab events, and checks where `document.activeElement` ends up after each one, across enough steps to find the boundary case. This is more expensive to run (it requires a live browser instance per test, not just a DOM parse) and still needs to know which elements constitute "the modal" and "the page behind it" — a judgment call for genuinely dynamic or unusually-structured modals. A more thorough tool could close much of this gap for straightforward cases; it's a matter of engineering investment rather than a hard theoretical limit the way alt-text quality is.

The honest answer to the engineering lead: yes to a heuristic improvement on alt text (worth doing, won't close the gap), and a qualified yes to interaction-simulation tooling for the keyboard trap (a real, different category of tool, worth evaluating, but manual testing remains the reliable check until it's proven out on Havenmark's actual components).

prompt: You're writing the methodology section of the Havenmark audit report — the part that explains to a non-technical stakeholder why the report contains more findings than their CI pipeline's automated scan ever has. Write two to three sentences that explain this accurately, without either (a) implying the CI scan is worthless, or (b) implying automated tooling is basically equivalent to manual testing with a small gap. Then name one concrete thing from this lesson you'd point to as evidence for your claim.
hints: Both extremes are wrong: the scan isn't worthless, and it isn't nearly-complete either. The accurate claim sits specifically in the middle, with a number attached.
A stakeholder unfamiliar with accessibility testing will likely default to one of the two wrong framings unless you're explicit about the actual coverage split.
Use a specific example from the audit (the size-picker, the discount badge, the countdown timer) rather than staying purely abstract.
explanation: A strong methodology paragraph does three things: states the automated scan's real, useful role (catching structural, syntactic issues like missing alt attributes and low contrast fast and consistently, which is why running it in CI is good practice and this audit didn't need to re-find every one of those), states the coverage limit precisely (roughly a third of WCAG success criteria are verifiable this way; the remaining two-thirds require simulating real interaction over time or judging meaning, which is what the manual passes in this report cover), and points to one concrete example that makes the gap tangible rather than abstract — e.g. "the site's CI scan reports zero critical issues, and separately, this audit found the primary size-selector is completely unreachable by keyboard, which blocks purchase entirely for keyboard-only and switch-access users — a defect no automated scan configuration could have caught, because the underlying markup is syntactically valid." This avoids both failure modes: it doesn't dismiss the scan (it explicitly credits what it does well) and it doesn't understate the gap (it names a specific, severe, scanner-invisible defect rather than a vague "there's more to check" gesture).
